stem: Mughal painting is essentially a blend of Persian and __________ traditions.
solution: Mughal painting blended Persian (Safavid) style with indigenous Indian traditions.

stem: The two Persian masters who founded the Mughal atelier under Humayun were Mir Sayyid Ali and __________.
solution: Mir Sayyid Ali and Abd-us-Samad were the Persian masters who founded the Mughal atelier.

stem: The first major Mughal illustrated manuscript, produced under Akbar, was the __________.
solution: The Hamzanama was the first great Mughal illustrated project under Akbar.

stem: The Mughal school truly flourished under the emperor __________.
solution: Mughal painting truly developed and flourished under Akbar.

stem: The Mughal painting under Jahangir is especially noted for its __________.
options: naturalism and studies of birds, animals and plants
solution: Under Jahangir, Mughal painting reached great naturalism, especially in nature studies.

stem: The Mughal artist famous for his masterly paintings of birds, animals and flowers was __________.
solution: Ustad Mansur was renowned for his naturalistic studies of birds, animals and flowers.

stem: Ustad Mansur was honoured by Jahangir with the title __________.
solution: Jahangir gave Mansur the title Nadir-ul-Asr, 'Wonder of the Age'.

stem: The Mughal painter Abul Hasan was given the title __________ by Jahangir.
solution: Abul Hasan received the title Nadir-uz-Zaman ('Wonder of the Time') from Jahangir.

stem: Mughal paintings were mostly created as __________.
solution: Mughal paintings were mainly book illustrations and album (muraqqa) portraits.

stem: A characteristic new subject introduced by Mughal painting was __________.
solution: Mughal painting introduced realistic individual portraiture to Indian art.

stem: European influence entered Mughal painting through prints brought by __________.
solution: European (Renaissance) influence entered via prints brought by Jesuit missionaries.

stem: One European technique adopted by Mughal painters was __________.
solution: Mughal painters adopted European shading and aerial perspective to suggest depth.

stem: The Mughal illustrated history of Akbar's reign is the __________.
solution: The Akbarnama, with its illustrated Ain-i-Akbari, records Akbar's reign.

stem: The Mughal painting reached its technical peak in refinement under __________.
solution: Under Shah Jahan, Mughal painting became highly refined, formal and jewel-like.

stem: Mughal painting declined under the emperor __________, who was uninterested in art.
solution: Mughal painting declined under Aurangzeb, who withdrew royal patronage.

stem: A Mughal painting was often the work of __________.
options: several specialised artists (one for outline, one for colour, one for faces)
solution: Mughal paintings were often collaborative, with specialists for outline, colour and portraits.

stem: The Mughal artists worked in the imperial workshop called the __________.
solution: Mughal artists worked in the imperial atelier, the tasvir khana / kitabkhana.

stem: The Hamzanama paintings were unusually __________ for Mughal miniatures.
solution: The Hamzanama paintings were unusually large for miniatures.

stem: Jahangir claimed he could identify the work of __________ within a single collaborative painting.
solution: Jahangir boasted he could recognise the hand of individual artists in a joint work.

stem: The 'Tutinama' (Tales of a Parrot) was an early illustrated manuscript of the __________ period.
solution: The Tutinama was an early Akbar-period illustrated manuscript.

stem: Mughal portraits often show the emperor with a __________ to signify divinity and glory.
solution: Mughal royal portraits often show a radiant halo signifying divine light and glory.

stem: The Mughal painting 'Jahangir Preferring a Sufi Shaikh to Kings' is by the artist __________.
solution: The allegorical painting 'Jahangir Preferring a Sufi Shaikh to Kings' is by Bichitr.

stem: Mughal paintings frequently depicted __________ scenes.
options: court, historical events, portraits and nature studies
solution: Mughal painting depicted court life, history, portraits and nature studies.

stem: The Mughal painter Bishandas was sent to __________ by Jahangir to paint a foreign ruler.
solution: Jahangir sent Bishandas to the Safavid court in Persia to paint Shah Abbas.

stem: Mughal painting used a __________ colour palette compared with the bold flat colours of Rajput painting.
solution: Mughal painting used a subtle, refined and naturalistic palette.

stem: The illustrated 'Padshahnama' records the reign of __________.
solution: The Padshahnama is the illustrated chronicle of Shah Jahan's reign.

stem: The 'Baburnama', the memoirs of Babur, was illustrated during the reign of __________.
solution: The Baburnama memoirs were illustrated during Akbar's reign.

stem: A key contribution of Jahangir to painting was the encouragement of __________.
solution: Jahangir encouraged detailed, scientific studies of flora and fauna.

stem: The Mughal album (a collection of paintings and calligraphy) is called a __________.
solution: A muraqqa is a Mughal album combining paintings and calligraphy.

stem: After the decline of the Mughal atelier, many artists migrated to __________ courts.
solution: As Mughal patronage declined, artists migrated to Rajput, Pahari and provincial courts.

stem: The Mughal painting tradition strongly influenced the __________ schools.
solution: Mughal painting influenced the Rajasthani, Pahari and Deccan schools.

stem: Mughal painting is characterised by fine __________ and attention to detail.
solution: Mughal painting is marked by fine line work and meticulous detail.

stem: The Mughal painters recorded the visit of __________ to Jahangir's court, showing European contact.
solution: European contact is reflected in the recording of English ambassadors at Jahangir's court.

stem: A famous naturalistic Mughal study by Mansur depicts the __________.
solution: Mansur painted famous studies such as the turkey cock, Siberian crane and a zebra.

stem: The Mughal school is important as a __________ of Indian, Persian and European art.
solution: Mughal painting is a rich synthesis of Indian, Persian and European elements.

stem: Mughal paintings depicting the emperor holding the world globe symbolise __________.
solution: The globe imagery symbolises the emperor's claim to universal dominion.

stem: The colours for Mughal painting were finely ground and applied with __________ brushes.
solution: Mughal painters used extremely fine brushes (often of squirrel hair) for detail.

stem: The Mughal 'darbar' (court) scenes served to __________.
options: glorify the emperor and record court hierarchy
solution: Court scenes glorified the emperor and recorded the hierarchy of the court.

stem: Mughal painting largely avoided the __________ that was central to Rajput painting.
solution: Mughal painting was more secular, avoiding the devotional focus central to Rajput art.

stem: The Mughal painting tradition flourished mainly from the __________ centuries.
solution: Mughal painting flourished mainly from the 16th to the 18th centuries.

stem: The Mughal painter Daswanth was a leading artist of __________'s atelier.
solution: Daswanth was a leading painter in Akbar's atelier.

stem: Mughal painting is generally __________ in scale.
solution: Mughal painting is a miniature (small-scale) art form.

stem: The 'jharokha darshan' portraits show the emperor at a __________.
solution: Jharokha darshan portraits show the emperor appearing at the palace balcony window.

stem: The Mughal painters' use of gold and jewel-like colour is most refined in the __________ period.
solution: The jewel-like, gold-rich refinement peaked in the Shah Jahan period.

stem: The Mughal painting tradition gave India its first great school of __________.
solution: The Mughal school introduced realistic, largely secular painting to India.

stem: Portraits in Mughal painting were usually shown in __________.
solution: Mughal portraits were usually rendered in profile.

stem: Mughal painting declined as royal patronage moved away, but its style survived in __________ centres.
solution: The Mughal style survived in provincial centres like Awadh, Murshidabad and Patna.

stem: The provincial continuation of Mughal painting under British influence produced the __________ style.
solution: The Mughal-derived, Europeanised provincial painting under the British is called the Company style.

stem: The Mughal school's greatest legacy is establishing __________ as a serious art in India.
solution: The Mughal school established portraiture and naturalistic observation as serious art.

stem: Mughal painting was patronised primarily by the __________.
solution: Mughal painting was patronised chiefly by the imperial court.
